First Warn Forecast
Saturday, August 15, 2026

FLASH FLOODING CONCERN THIS MORNING

DANGEROUS HEAT CONTINUES THIS WEEKEND

RELIEF FINALLY BEGINS TO ARRIVE EARLY NEXT WEEK

Good Saturday morning! We have a couple of weather stories to talk about today, and depending on where you live across the First Warn Weather area, your weather may look quite different. Heavy rain and a localized flash flooding threat remain concerns to our north and east this morning, while Central Missouri, the St. Louis area, Southeast Missouri and Southern Illinois deal with another round of dangerous August heat and humidity.

Thunderstorms have been producing some impressive rainfall rates across northeast Missouri and west-central Illinois early this morning. We are talking rainfall rates of 1 to 2 inches per hour, and possibly higher underneath some of the stronger storms. There is a tremendous amount of moisture available in the atmosphere, so these thunderstorms are very efficient rain producers. The greatest flash flooding concern should remain north of the St. Louis area through mid-morning.

Once the morning thunderstorms settle down, our attention goes right back to the heat. And yes, unfortunately, we have another very hot Saturday ahead.

Across Central Missouri, including Columbia, Jefferson City and the Lake of the Ozarks, expect another hot and humid afternoon. Temperatures will climb into the 90s, but the humidity will make it feel considerably hotter. Heat index values around 105 degrees or higher will be possible, particularly as you head south toward the Lake. Most of Central Missouri should stay dry through the afternoon, although I cannot completely rule out a stray shower.

The St. Louis metro will also remain firmly stuck in the heat and humidity today. Temperatures will climb into the 90s with heat index values potentially reaching 105 to 110 degrees. Some communities north of the metro could catch a little temporary relief from cloud cover or rain-cooled air, but for most of St. Louis and the surrounding area, this is another day to take the heat seriously.

Southeast Missouri will probably have some of the hottest conditions across our coverage area today. Farmington, Fredericktown, Cape Girardeau, Poplar Bluff and surrounding communities are unlikely to get much help from the clouds and rain-cooled air farther north. Expect another afternoon with heat index values around or above 105 degrees in many locations.

Southern Illinois will see some variation depending on how far north or south you are. Areas closer to the I-70 corridor could occasionally benefit from clouds and thunderstorm outflow, while farther south toward Mt. Vernon, Marion and Carbondale, the heat and humidity will remain firmly in place. Heat index values over 100 degrees are likely, with some areas potentially approaching 105 degrees or higher.

Tonight we will have to watch northern Missouri and portions of Illinois again. Another round of thunderstorms may develop as the low-level jet strengthens overnight. Rain chances increase to around 40 to 60 percent in these areas. Confidence in exactly where the heaviest rain sets up remains relatively low, but with the atmosphere still loaded with moisture, torrential rainfall will again be possible.

That is especially important in places that receive heavy rain this morning. It will not take much additional rainfall tonight to cause problems where the ground is already saturated. If storms repeatedly move over the same locations, flash flooding could quickly become a concern again.

Then comes Sunday, and finally we can start talking about some changes.

A cold front will begin pushing south through Missouri and Illinois. The problem is that it is not exactly in a hurry. Northern portions of the region will notice the improvement first, while areas farther south may have to endure one more hot and humid day.

Central Missouri should gradually see some improvement Sunday as the front works south. Columbia and areas farther north will have the better opportunity for relief first, while Jefferson City and especially the Lake of the Ozarks may remain hot and humid longer.

For the St. Louis area, Sunday looks like a transition day. It will still be hot and humid, but the approaching front will bring increasing chances for scattered showers and thunderstorms, particularly later Sunday afternoon and evening. Heavy rain and some gusty winds will be possible with the stronger storms.

Southeast Missouri will likely be one of the last areas to get meaningful relief. Another very hot and humid Sunday is expected, and depending on where the front eventually stalls, portions of Southeast Missouri could still flirt with heat index values around 100 to 105 degrees Monday or Tuesday.

Southern Illinois should also begin seeing some changes Sunday as the front settles south. Scattered thunderstorms will be possible, especially later in the day, followed by gradually improving temperatures and humidity heading into Monday.

By Monday and Tuesday, most of us should finally get a break. Temperatures will come down, humidity levels should become more manageable, and after this prolonged stretch of oppressive August weather, it is going to feel pretty good. Southeast Missouri may hold onto the heat a little longer depending on exactly where the front stalls.

We are not completely finished with active weather next week. Another stronger disturbance and cold front should approach sometime Tuesday night into Wednesday. That will bring another chance for showers and thunderstorms across Central Missouri, the St. Louis area, Southeast Missouri and Southern Illinois. There could eventually be a few stronger storms involved, but there is still plenty of uncertainty with the timing.

For today, we get through one more round of dangerous heat. Drink plenty of water, take breaks if you are working outside, check on your neighbors and family members, and remember the pavement is brutally hot for our four-legged friends.

And for those of you who have been asking when this heat finally gives us a break, I have some good news.

We are getting there.

Monday is looking better.

severeNarrative:
First Warn Forecast & Severe Weather Outlook Update
11:50 AM CDT | Wednesday, June 17, 2026
First Warn Weather Alert Day
Headlines
Severe thunderstorms remain likely this afternoon and evening across Missouri and Illinois.
Damaging winds up to 85 mph, large hail up to 2.5 inches, and several tornadoes remain possible.
The greatest threat locally remains across eastern and central Missouri and western Illinois, including the St. Louis metro area.
Strong southwest winds will gust between 40 and 50 mph outside of thunderstorms.
Peak severe weather threat for the St. Louis area remains between 6 PM and 9 PM.

A potentially dangerous severe weather outbreak remains on track across portions of Missouri and Illinois this afternoon and evening. There has been little change in the overall forecast since this morning. The Storm Prediction Center continues to highlight much of eastern and central Missouri and western Illinois in an Enhanced Risk (Level 3 of 5) for severe weather, while portions of central Illinois remain under a Moderate Risk (Level 4 of 5) where the highest threat for significant severe weather exists.

An intense cluster of thunderstorms that developed overnight across Iowa produced wind gusts exceeding 90 mph and continues to influence the forecast across Illinois late this morning. The primary outflow boundary currently extends from far northeast Missouri into portions of south-central Illinois. This boundary will likely serve as a focus for severe thunderstorm development later today.

Strong sunshine south of the boundary is allowing temperatures to rapidly climb through the 80s while dew points remain in the upper 60s and lower 70s. Combined with an exceptionally strong wind field aloft, conditions remain favorable for supercells capable of producing all severe weather hazards.

While morning storms may slightly alter where the greatest risk ultimately develops, confidence remains high that numerous severe thunderstorms will develop this afternoon and continue through the evening hours.

Primary Threats

🌪 Several Tornadoes Possible

A few strong tornadoes remain possible.
Greatest tornado threat remains across central Illinois.
Tornadoes remain possible across eastern Missouri and western Illinois, especially near any lingering outflow boundaries.

💨 Destructive Winds Possible

Widespread damaging winds of 60 to 80 mph.
Isolated wind gusts exceeding 85 mph remain possible.
Significant tree damage and widespread power outages could occur.

🧊 Large to Very Large Hail

Large hail remains possible with discrete supercells.
Hailstones up to 2.5 inches in diameter may occur.
Timing Across Missouri and Illinois
1 PM - 3 PM

The first severe thunderstorms are expected to develop across northeast Missouri and portions of west-central Illinois. Areas near Quincy, Kirksville, Palmyra, Hannibal, and surrounding communities should closely monitor conditions.

3 PM - 6 PM

The severe weather threat expands southeast into central Missouri and western Illinois. Columbia, Jefferson City, Mexico, Bowling Green, Troy, and portions of the northern St. Louis metro could see supercells capable of producing tornadoes, very large hail, and destructive winds.

6 PM - 9 PM

This remains the peak severe weather window for the St. Louis metropolitan area and much of eastern Missouri and western Illinois. Storms may become more widespread during this period while maintaining the potential to produce damaging winds, large hail, and tornadoes. Residents from St. Louis and St. Charles to Edwardsville, Belleville, Alton, Farmington, and surrounding communities should be prepared to act quickly if warnings are issued.

9 PM - Midnight

Storms are expected to organize into a line extending from central Missouri into southern Indiana. Damaging straight-line winds become the primary threat as storms shift into southeast Missouri and southern Illinois. Heavy rainfall and localized flooding may also develop overnight.

Local First Warn Outlook

The highest confidence for severe weather today exists across the Enhanced Risk area covering much of eastern and central Missouri, including Columbia, Jefferson City, the St. Louis metro, northeast Missouri, and west-central Illinois.

Farther south, a Slight Risk extends across southern Missouri and southern Illinois, including Rolla, Salem, Farmington, Fredericktown, Marion, and Mount Vernon. Severe thunderstorms remain possible in these areas, but storm coverage and intensity may be somewhat lower than locations farther north.

The lowest severe weather threat remains across the Missouri Bootheel and far southern Illinois near the Kentucky border where a Marginal Risk remains in place. However, isolated severe storms cannot be ruled out.

Missouri Bootheel

Additional Concern: Strong Winds Outside of Storms

Even outside of thunderstorms, strong southwest winds will continue through the afternoon. Sustained winds of 20 to 30 mph with gusts of 40 to 50 mph are expected. Loose outdoor objects should be secured, and travel may become difficult for high-profile vehicles.

Thursday Outlook

The cold front responsible for today's severe weather will gradually move south of the region overnight. Showers and a few thunderstorms may linger into Thursday, especially across southeast Missouri and southwest Illinois. Cooler temperatures in the 70s and lower 80s will provide a welcome break from today's heat and humidity.

Bottom Line

There has been little change in the forecast thinking since this morning. The atmosphere remains primed for severe thunderstorm development this afternoon and evening. While the greatest threat for strong tornadoes remains across central Illinois, all severe weather hazards remain possible across eastern Missouri and western Illinois.

The St. Louis metro remains in the corridor for severe weather between 6 PM and 9 PM, with damaging winds, large hail, and tornadoes all possible. Everyone across the First Warn viewing area should remain weather aware and have multiple ways to receive warnings throughout the day and tonight.
